section.title: The Deserted City
section.sectionRationale: The book opens with a funeral dirge over Jerusalem. The first acrostic poem walks slowly through the ruined city: a widow who was once a queen, roads that mourn because no one comes to the feasts, and a people led away captive. Halfway through, the voice shifts from a narrator describing Zion to Zion herself speaking, owning her sin and crying out to the LORD.
section.thesis: Jerusalem sits deserted and disgraced because of her own transgressions; yet even in her ruin she turns from her useless lovers to the LORD, confesses that He is righteous, and pleads with Him to look on her affliction.
section.frameNote: Two halves. First, the narrator surveys the deserted city, its emptiness, its shame, and the hand of the LORD behind it, 1:1 to 11. Then Zion herself speaks, confessing her rebellion, owning that God is righteous, and begging Him to see her sorrow, 1:12 to 22.

units.label: The city sits alone
units.note: a widow who was once a queen

verses.text: {{eykah|How}} lonely lies the city, once so full of people! She who was great among the nations has become a widow. The princess of the provinces has become a slave.
She weeps aloud in the night, with tears upon her cheeks. Among all her lovers there is no one to {{nacham|comfort}} her. All her friends have betrayed her; they have become her enemies.
Judah has gone into exile under affliction and harsh slavery; she dwells among the nations but finds no place to rest. All her pursuers have overtaken her in the midst of her distress.
The roads to Zion mourn, because no one comes to her appointed feasts. All her gates are deserted; her priests groan, her maidens grieve, and she herself is bitter with anguish.
Her foes have become her masters; her enemies are at ease. For the LORD has brought her grief because of her many {{pesha|transgressions}}. Her children have gone away as captives before the enemy.
All the splendor has departed from the Daughter of Zion. Her princes are like deer that find no pasture; they lack the strength to flee in the face of the hunter.

units.label: Her shame and the LORD's hand

verses.text: In the days of her affliction and wandering Jerusalem remembers all the treasures that were hers in days of old. When her people fell into enemy hands she received no help. Her enemies looked upon her, laughing at her downfall.
Jerusalem has sinned greatly; therefore she has become an object of scorn. All who honored her now despise her, for they have seen her nakedness; she herself groans and turns away.
Her uncleanness stains her skirts; she did not consider her end. Her downfall was astounding; there was no one to comfort her. Look, O LORD, on my affliction, for the enemy has triumphed!
The adversary has seized all her treasures. For she has seen the nations enter her sanctuary, those You had forbidden to enter Your assembly.
All her people groan as they search for bread. They have traded their treasures for food to keep themselves alive. Look, O LORD, and consider, for I have become despised.

units.label: Zion speaks: is there any sorrow like mine?
units.note: the day of His fierce anger

verses.text: Is this nothing to you, all you who pass by? Look around and see! Is there any sorrow like mine, which was inflicted on me, which the LORD made me suffer on the day of His fierce anger?
He sent fire from on high, and it overpowered my bones. He spread a net for my feet and turned me back. He made me desolate, faint all the day long.

My {{pesha|transgressions}} are bound into a yoke, knit together by His hand; they are draped over my neck, and the Lord has broken my strength. He has delivered me into the hands of those I cannot withstand.
The Lord has rejected all the mighty men in my midst; He has summoned an army against me to crush my young warriors. Like grapes in a winepress, the Lord has trampled the Virgin Daughter of Judah.
For these things I weep; my eyes flow with tears. For there is no one nearby to {{nacham|comfort}} me, no one to revive my soul. My children are destitute because the enemy has prevailed.
Zion stretches out her hands, but there is no one to comfort her. The LORD has decreed against Jacob that his neighbors become his foes. Jerusalem has become an unclean thing among them.

units.label: The LORD is righteous: a plea for justice

verses.text: The LORD is righteous, yet I rebelled against His command. Listen, all you people; look upon my suffering. My young men and maidens have gone into captivity.
I called out to my lovers, but they have betrayed me. My priests and elders perished in the city while they searched for food to keep themselves alive.
See, O LORD, how distressed I am! I am churning within; my heart is pounding within me, for I have been most rebellious. Outside, the sword bereaves; inside, there is death.

People have heard my groaning, but there is no one to comfort me. All my enemies have heard of my trouble; they are glad that You have caused it. May You bring the day You have announced, so that they may become like me.
Let all their wickedness come before You, and deal with them as You have dealt with me because of all my {{pesha|transgressions}}. For my groans are many, and my heart is faint.

eykah.gloss: How, or Alas. This single word of stunned grief opens the poem and gives the book its Hebrew name. It is the cry of a mourner at a graveside, staring at ruin and asking how it could come to this.

nacham.gloss: To comfort or console. The refrain there is no one to comfort her runs through the chapter like a bell tolling. Every human comforter has failed, and the ache of the whole book is the longing for a comfort that only God can finally give.

pesha.gloss: Transgression, rebellion, a deliberate breaking with rightful authority. It is stronger than a mere mistake: it names sin as revolt against the LORD. Zion does not blame fate or her enemies alone; she confesses that her many transgressions are why she suffers.

basic.context: Lamentations opens like a funeral song sung over a dead body, except the body is a city. Jerusalem has been destroyed by Babylon in 586 BC, the temple burned, the people dragged into exile. The poet walks through the empty streets and weeps: the city that was once a queen among the nations is now a widow, alone, betrayed by her allies, with no one to comfort her. Then, in the middle, the city herself begins to speak. She does not deny her guilt. She admits that the LORD is righteous and that her own rebellion brought this down. And she keeps crying out for God to look and see.
basic.hermeneutics: This is real grief put into careful poetry, an acrostic that runs through the Hebrew alphabet, as if to say the sorrow is complete, from A to Z. It is important to read it as honest lament, not despair without God. The city grieves and confesses in the same breath. The key question is: how do God's people mourn when the disaster is deserved? The answer here is to weep truthfully, own the sin, refuse the false comforters, and turn the whole crushing weight of it toward the LORD.
basic.originalLanguages: The book is named for its first word, eykah, How, or Alas, the gasp of a mourner. Again and again we hear there is no one to comfort her, from the root nacham, and that aching for comfort is the pulse of the book. The reason for the ruin is named plainly with the word pesha, transgression, which means rebellion, not just a slip. Zion owns her rebellion even as she grieves its cost.
basic.typology: The deserted city, struck under the anger of God for sin, points forward to the true and greater grief of the cross, where Jesus bears the wrath our sin deserves. The cry Is there any sorrow like mine has long been heard by the church on the lips of the suffering Christ. And the longing for a comforter is answered when Jesus promises the Comforter, the Spirit, and when God finally wipes away every tear.
basic.christ: Jerusalem's cry, Is there any sorrow like mine, is answered most deeply not by the city but by Christ, the man of sorrows, who enters the God forsaken place we deserved. Jesus wept over this same Jerusalem. He bears the fierce anger of God against transgression so that His people might be comforted. Where Zion had no one to comfort her, Christ becomes our comfort and sends the Comforter.
basic.god: God is holy and just: the destruction is not random, it is His righteous response to persistent rebellion, and Zion says so plainly, the LORD is righteous. Yet He is not absent. He is the One being cried out to, again and again, Look, O LORD. Even the appeal for Him to see is an act of faith that He is there and that He cares.
basic.crossReferences: Jeremiah 52 records the fall of Jerusalem this poem mourns. Luke 19 shows Jesus weeping over the city. Isaiah 53 gives us the man of sorrows who bears our grief. John 14 promises the Comforter, and Revelation 21 promises the day when God wipes away every tear.
basic.oneStory: This is the low point of the Old Testament story: the city of God in ruins because of sin, exactly as the covenant warned. Yet the honest grief and confession here already reach toward the LORD, and the whole Bible answers the cry for a comforter in Jesus, the man of sorrows who bears the judgment and turns mourning into joy.

context.literary:
Lamentations 1 is built with care, and its care is part of its meaning. Each of its twenty-two verses begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and each verse has three lines, so the grief is held inside a strict frame. In chapters 2, 3 and 4 the poet puts the letter pe before ayin; here the order is the usual one, as the opening words of verses 16 and 17 show. Verse 3 begins with the word for exile, galetah, and verse 1 with the gasp of the book's title.

The poem has two voices. In verses 1 to 11 a narrator describes the city in the third person, and in verses 12 to 22 Zion speaks in the first. The division is not clean. Twice in the narrator's half the city breaks in with a prayer, 'Look, O LORD, on my affliction,' verse 9, and 'Look, O LORD, and consider,' verse 11, as if the poet cannot keep her out. Then in verse 12 she turns and addresses the passers-by, and in verse 18 she addresses God and all peoples at once.

A refrain holds the poem together: 'there is no one to comfort her,' in verses 2, 9, 16, 17 and 21. The city's loneliness is stated five times and is never relieved within the chapter. The poem is built on personification, with the city as a bereaved woman, a widow, a mother, a rejected wife, and it is that woman, not the ruined stones, who is brought to speak. The ending is unresolved on purpose: verse 22 closes with groaning and a faint heart, and the book does not turn until chapter 3.
context.historical:
The poem looks back on the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, and its wording suggests it was composed soon afterwards, by someone who had seen the city. Verse 4 says no one comes to the appointed feasts. Yet Jeremiah 41:5 records that eighty men from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria, shaved and torn and cut, still walked toward the ruined house of the LORD with grain offerings and incense, a sign of how much the broken sanctuary still meant. Mourning, not festival, filled the roads to Zion.

The 'lovers' of verses 2 and 19 are the political allies Judah courted instead of trusting the LORD. Neighbouring states had been invited to join the revolt, Jeremiah 27:3, Egypt had promised help, Jeremiah 37:5-7, and Edom later gloated over the ruin, Psalm 137:7. None of them intervened when it mattered. Jeremiah 30:14 uses the same language of a faithless people whose lovers have forgotten them.

Verse 10 says the nations entered the sanctuary that the LORD had forbidden them to enter. The reference is probably to Deuteronomy 23:3, which barred Ammonites and Moabites from the assembly; to a priestly poet, the sight of foreign soldiers in the holy place was the worst of all losses.

The poem belongs to a community still in the land. Many had gone into exile, but the poor had been left, and the leaders had been executed, Jeremiah 52:16 and 52:24-27. The famine of verses 11 and 19 matches Jeremiah 52:6. It is also worth knowing that Jewish worship has read Lamentations on the ninth of Av, the day that came to be the memorial of both temples' destruction.
context.canonical:
This chapter is the grief that Moses predicted. Leviticus 26:31-33 says cities would be left in rubble, sanctuaries laid waste, and the people scattered, and Deuteronomy 28 adds siege, hunger and captivity; the poem works as the sufferer's own testimony that these were not empty threats. Jeremiah had already summoned wailing women to teach 'a lament over us,' Jeremiah 9:17-18, and Lamentations is the lament those women were asked to sing.

The language of comfort in this chapter reaches its answer in Isaiah. Where the poem says five times that there is no comforter, Isaiah 40:1 opens with 'Comfort, comfort My people,' and Isaiah 66:13 promises 'As a mother comforts her son, so will I comfort you.' The widow of Lamentations 1:1 is told in Isaiah 54:4-5 that she will forget the reproach of her widowhood, for her Maker is her husband.

Psalms 74, 79 and 137 are close companions, since each grieves the same destruction in prayer. In the New Testament the thread is gathered by Jesus: He grieves over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41-44, warns of her coming siege, Luke 21:20-24, and says that those who mourn will be comforted, Matthew 5:4. Paul calls God 'the God of all comfort,' 2 Corinthians 1:3-4. And Revelation 21:4 promises that God will wipe every tear from their eyes.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet is not trying to explain the disaster so much as to give a stunned people words to say to God. Grief of this size can leave a community silent, and silence in front of the LORD is a kind of unbelief. By setting the weeping inside a form that every Israelite child could memorise, he makes it possible to grieve together and to grieve in prayer. He wants the people to say both things at once, that the LORD is righteous, verse 18, and that the pain is real and no one has comforted them.

He also wants an honest account of guilt. The city is allowed to name her faults, verses 5, 8, 14, 18 and 20, but she is also allowed to say that her enemies are cruel and that they should answer for it, verses 21 and 22. Neither confession cancels the other. The poem is trying to keep a nation from two false ways of coping: blaming only others, and blaming only itself until nothing is left to pray with.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Lamentations records the speech of a city in agony, and not all of it is meant to be copied. The wish in verses 21 and 22 that her enemies 'become like me' is the cry of the wounded, put into the mouth of the poem so that it can be handed to God rather than acted out. Scripture does not turn it into a command to take revenge; Deuteronomy 32:35 and Romans 12:19 reserve vengeance to the Lord.

In the same way, the poem explains this particular catastrophe by this particular covenant people's rebellion. It does not teach that every sufferer is being punished for sin, a view that the book of Job and John 9:3 reject. What carries forward is the pattern of prayer: tell God exactly what has happened, own what is yours to own, and keep addressing Him by name until He answers.

debates.question: Who wrote Lamentations?

views.label: Jeremiah
views.case: Jewish and Christian tradition has long assigned the book to Jeremiah. The Greek Bible opens it with a note that Jeremiah sat weeping, and 2 Chronicles 35:25 records that he composed laments for Josiah. The themes of weeping and sieges fit Jeremiah 8:21 to 9:1.

views.label: An anonymous eyewitness
views.case: The Hebrew text names no author, and the poems use a form and vocabulary somewhat different from the prophet's style. On this view an unnamed survivor, perhaps a priest or temple singer, wrote soon after 586 BC.

views.label: A circle of poets
views.case: The five poems differ in form, from the three-line acrostic to the single-verse acrostic of chapter 4 to the non-acrostic fifth, and some propose several hands or one author across a longer span.

debates.bearing: The meaning of the poem does not hang on the answer. Whoever the poet was, he stood among the ruins and wrote as a believer, and the book was received as Scripture by those who recognised its voice.

debates.question: How should the prayer of verses 21 and 22 be read?

views.label: A righteous plea for justice
views.case: The poet asks for no more than God's own principle in Deuteronomy 32:35, that wrongs will be repaid. The enemies were cruel beyond their commission, Zechariah 1:15, and to ask God to judge them is to hand vengeance over to Him.

views.label: A raw outburst that Scripture leaves unfinished
views.case: The prayer is real emotion, preserved because honest grief includes anger, but it is not an ideal. The book itself turns toward humility and confession in chapter 3, and the New Testament teaches love for enemies, Matthew 5:44.

views.label: A prayer that sees the nations judged too
views.case: Verse 22 asks for treatment equal to Zion's. The same God who judges His own people will not exempt others, as Jeremiah 25:12 and 51:24 say, and the cry points forward to Revelation 6:10, where the martyrs ask how long.

debates.bearing: All three can be true together. The prayer is permitted because it is spoken to God and not acted on by the speaker, and its answer is found in the cross, where justice and mercy are both satisfied.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 says the city 'lies lonely,' and the Hebrew is a verb for sitting, yashvah, followed by the word badad, 'alone.' Badad is a word with a history. In the blessing of Moses the Hebrew of Deuteronomy 33:28 pairs 'dwells securely' with this word, and Balaam says of Israel that she is a people who 'dwell apart,' Numbers 23:9, in the same vein. The word that described Israel's safe distinctness now describes her desertion. Lamentations 3:28 will use the phrase again, 'let him sit alone in silence,' so that the posture of the abandoned city becomes the posture of repentant waiting.

The same verse says the princess has become a slave, and the underlying noun is mas, forced labour. It is the word used of the Egyptians' 'forced labor' of Israel in Exodus 1:11. The people who were brought out of corvée in Egypt are back under it. The verse also says the city is 'like a widow,' ke-almanah. The Hebrew carries a comparison, since the city is not literally widowed; her husband, the LORD, is not dead, and Isaiah 54:4-5 treats her widowhood as a state to be reversed.

A key word returns three times in the chapter, oni, 'affliction,' in verses 3, 7 and 9. It is the word the LORD uses in Exodus 3:7, 'I have indeed seen the affliction of My people.' So the plea in verse 9, 'Look, O LORD, on my affliction,' is a prayer in the very words of the exodus, asking Him to do again what He did in Egypt. Deuteronomy 26:7 makes the same link.

Verse 17 calls Jerusalem 'an unclean thing,' niddah, a word for the ritual impurity of a woman in Leviticus 15:19-24. Ezekiel 36:17 uses it of Israel's behaviour, 'the uncleanness of a woman's impurity.' Verse 9 adds that her uncleanness 'stains her skirts.' The city is treated as a woman no one will touch.

In verses 12 and 22 the poet uses the verb 'alal, translated 'inflicted' and 'dealt.' It also means to glean a vine thoroughly, as in Leviticus 19:10, and it is used with a vineyard's picking in mind. That fits verse 15, where the Lord 'has trampled' the Virgin Daughter of Judah 'like grapes in a winepress.' The one who gleans the vines and treads the grapes is the LORD Himself.

Finally, the name of the book, eykah, is made of the same four consonants as the 'Where are you?' of Genesis 3:9, ayyekah, though vowelled differently. Jewish readers have long noticed the echo. The first question God asked a sinner is answered, in a way, by a people who ask how the LORD's city has fallen.

typology.type: The widowed city who will be called a bride, verse 1
typology.fulfillment: Jerusalem sits like a widow, her husband silent and her lovers gone. Isaiah 54:4-5 reverses the picture, telling her to forget her widowhood because her Maker is her husband. The New Testament carries it forward: Christ loves the church as a bridegroom loves a bride, Ephesians 5:25-27, and the redeemed city comes down 'as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband,' Revelation 21:2. The type falls short because Zion's restoration depended on a covenant she kept breaking, whereas the new Jerusalem is made spotless by the Husband's own sacrifice.

The city's sins are 'bound into a yoke' and draped over her neck, so that sin is felt as a weight too heavy to carry. Isaiah 53:6 says that the LORD has laid on the servant 'the iniquity of us all,' and 1 Peter 2:24 says that Christ bore our sins in His body on the tree. Jesus invites the weary to take His yoke upon them, Matthew 11:28-30, because He has already taken theirs. The type falls short because Zion carried her own sin and was crushed by it, whereas the Servant carries sin that is not His and is not destroyed.

typology.type: The winepress of the LORD's anger, verse 15
typology.fulfillment: The Lord has trampled the Virgin Daughter of Judah 'like grapes in a winepress.' The picture is of anger poured out on His own people. Isaiah 63:3 shows a lone figure treading the winepress in fury, and Revelation 19:15 shows Christ treading 'the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty.' The escalation is that, on the cross, the One who judges also stands in the place of the judged. The correspondence is a fair echo rather than a declared type, since the New Testament does not quote Lamentations here.

typology.type: The nations in the sanctuary and the unclean city, verses 10 and 17
typology.fulfillment: Foreigners walk into the holy place and the city is treated as unclean. Jesus enters the same temple in Matthew 21:12-13 and drives out those who made it a den of robbers, quoting Jeremiah 7:11. He is the true priest who cleanses, and the one who touches the unclean and makes them clean, Mark 1:41. The link is an echo and should be held loosely, but it points to the One who restores what the exile could only mourn.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the figure of the one who weeps over Jerusalem. The woman who cries 'Is this nothing to you, all you who pass by?' in verse 12 is answered, centuries later, by a man who looks at the same city from the Mount of Olives and weeps, Luke 19:41-44. He foretells her siege, Luke 21:20-24, and the language is that of Lamentations: foes surrounding, children dashed down, a city that did not know the time of her visitation. Where the poem found no one to comfort her, Jesus does not turn away from the city that had killed the prophets, and He grieves over the very desolation His own word predicts.

It leads to Christ through the yoke and the winepress. In verse 14 Zion's transgressions are bound into a yoke that breaks her strength, and in verse 15 the Lord treads her like grapes. Both pictures reappear in the work of Christ. Isaiah 53:6 and 1 Peter 2:24 describe the Servant bearing the sins that the city could not bear, and Revelation 19:15 shows the same Lord treading the winepress of wrath. The pages of Scripture hold both the Judge who carries out the sentence and the Substitute who takes it.

It leads to Christ through the missing comforter. Jesus is the answer to the question the poem keeps asking. He promises 'another Helper,' the Spirit of truth, John 14:16, and He declares that those who mourn will be comforted, Matthew 5:4. Paul calls the Father the 'God of all comfort' who comforts us in all our troubles, 2 Corinthians 1:3-4. The five-fold 'no one to comfort her' is met by a God who ends in Revelation 21:4 by wiping away every tear.

It leads to Christ through the pattern of the afflicted one. The poem puts the weight of Zion's suffering in the first person: 'Is there any sorrow like mine, which was inflicted on me?' The church has read this on Christ's lips in Holy Week, because the Gospels show Him as a man of sorrows, Isaiah 53:3, struck down and afflicted, who was left alone while those who passed by shook their heads, Matthew 27:39. A caution is needed. Zion's suffering is the result of her own sin, verses 5 and 18, while Christ's is not, so the link is not that the two sufferers are the same but that He enters the very place she occupied and bears what she deserved.
study.god:
The chapter makes the hard claim that the LORD is the author of what has happened. 'The LORD has brought her grief,' verse 5, and the city says that He sent fire, spread a net and trampled her, verses 13 to 15. The poem does not hide behind the army of Babylon. It confesses that the world is governed by a God whose threats in Deuteronomy are as real as His promises, so that nothing falls outside His hand, not even this.

It shows a God who is righteous. The most surprising line in the chapter comes in verse 18: 'The LORD is righteous, for I have rebelled against His command.' The city does not say that she was treated fairly by the world, only that she was treated justly by the LORD. This confession, made in the middle of agony, is a form of worship. It means that the God she is crying to is not a tyrant and that His verdict is not arbitrary.

It shows a God who is addressed even when He seems absent. The prayers 'Look, O LORD,' verses 9, 11 and 20, assume that He can see. He is called on to see what He has done, and the very asking holds that He is not indifferent. The exodus word 'affliction' in verse 9 implies that this is the God who saw Israel's misery in Egypt, Exodus 3:7, and who heard the groaning of His people.

It shows the tension between judgment and mercy that the book holds without resolving. Judgment is written in the verbs of verses 13 to 15, but the very form of the poem, a prayer, expresses a hope that the God who struck can also heal. Hosea 6:1 states the same logic: 'He has torn us to pieces, but He will heal us.' Mercy has not yet appeared in chapter 1, yet the book's central chapter will say that it has been there all along.

For worship, this chapter teaches that praise and grief are not opposites. A people can say 'the LORD is righteous' with tears running down. It teaches the church to bring lament to God and not to sing only the easy songs. And it warns against treating God as a distant explanation. The God of this chapter is near enough to be addressed, to be asked to look, and to be held to what He has promised.

crossReferences.note: The covenant warning that the LORD would reduce cities to rubble, lay waste sanctuaries and scatter the people. The poem is the experience behind that warning, which is why verses 5, 8 and 18 treat the disaster as the answer to rebellion and not as an accident.

Moses says that siege and famine would drive people to desperate measures if they would not serve the LORD joyfully. The famine in verses 11 and 19, with people trading treasures for food, is a picture of those curses being fulfilled.

The historical record of the fall that this poem mourns. Where Jeremiah 52 counts cubits, bronze and head counts, Lamentations 1 gives the inner experience of the same event, the sense of being abandoned by lovers and friends.

The prophet uses the same image of a faithless city whose lovers have forgotten her, and says that the LORD Himself struck her for her great iniquity. It sharpens the poem's point: the lovers who betrayed her in verses 2 and 19 were not her real enemy.

The LORD says He has seen the affliction of His people in Egypt, and the word 'affliction' is the same one used in Lamentations 1:9. The poet is praying the exodus formula, asking God to look at His people again as He once did in Egypt.

Where Lamentations 1 says five times that there is no comforter, Isaiah opens with the command, 'Comfort, comfort My people.' The verse is the poem's answer in the same vocabulary: forced labor completed, iniquity pardoned, the exile turned toward return.

The city who sat like a widow is told that she will forget the shame of her widowhood, because her Maker is her husband. Isaiah answers the image of Lamentations 1:1 directly and promises the change of status that the exile seems to have ended.

A figure treads the winepress alone in anger, so that his garments are stained. It is the same image as Lamentations 1:15, but now the treading is directed against the nations, which shows how the picture of anger can be turned to rescue.

God's first question to a sinner, 'Where are you?', has the same consonants as the book's opening word, 'How.' Hearing the echo, the reader can take the poem as a question of loss that answers a question of rebellion, the long consequence of leaving the garden.

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem as He draws near. The scene reads like the poem's first verses put into action, with the prophet weeping, the city warned and the coming siege described. It shows that the grief of Lamentations is shared by the Lord Himself.

Jesus promises that those who mourn will be comforted. The beatitude takes the poem's refrain of no comforter and promises a comforter, so that the mourning of the exile is not wasted but is the doorway to blessing.

God will wipe away every tear, and death and mourning and crying and pain will be no more. The final answer to the weeping city, and to every verse in which the poet's eyes flow with tears, is the end of weeping, not its management.

study.oneStory:
The first chapter of Lamentations is the Bible's creation story run in reverse. A garden city that was once full of people sits alone. A woman who was given a husband, a house and a name is a widow, a slave and a thing no one will touch. The sanctuary where God had met His people is entered by the nations. The structure of Genesis 1 to 3, of blessing and then fall, has come round again at the scale of a nation, and the exile east of the sanctuary is an echo of the expulsion east of Eden, Genesis 3:24.

The poem also looks back to the exodus. The people who were once brought out of forced labour are in forced labour again, and the poet's prayer uses the exodus word for affliction. This is the pattern of the Old Testament: redemption, rebellion, a return to bondage, and a cry for redemption. The prophets answer the cry with a new exodus, and Isaiah 40:1 begins with comfort for exactly the people whom Lamentations 1 leaves with none.

What the poem lacks is any mechanism for the problem it names. The city can confess, 'the LORD is righteous,' and can ask for God to look, but she cannot make the transgressions that are bound into a yoke any lighter. The rest of the Bible supplies what she cannot. A servant bears the iniquity of us all, Isaiah 53:6. A Son weeps over the city and then goes up to it to die. The Spirit is sent as another comforter, John 14:16.

The story ends where the poem could not go. In the new creation the city that sat alone is a bride adorned for her husband, and the tears she wept in verse 2 are wiped away by God Himself, Revelation 21:2-4. The hardest chapter of the exile is not left standing alone; it is the lowest point of a story whose last page undoes every line of it.

quiz.q: What kind of writing is Lamentations 1?

options.text: A funeral dirge over the fallen city, shaped as an alphabetical acrostic of grief.
options.note: The poem mourns Jerusalem verse by verse through the Hebrew alphabet, ordered grief from A to Z.

options.text: A poem of sorrow over Jerusalem's destruction.
options.note: True to its content, though it misses the deliberate acrostic form that structures the lament.

options.text: A record of laws for rebuilding the temple.
options.note: It is grief and confession, not legal instruction.

options.text: A victory song celebrating Babylon's triumph.
options.note: It weeps over the ruin; it does not celebrate the conqueror.

quiz.q: Why does the poem say the disaster came upon Jerusalem?

options.text: Because of her many transgressions; the LORD is righteous and she rebelled against His command.
options.note: The poem names sin plainly, 1:5 and 1:18, and Zion confesses it.

options.text: Because God brought grief on her for her sin.
options.note: Correct, though it leaves out Zion's own confession that the LORD is righteous.

options.text: Because her enemies were simply stronger than her.
options.note: Babylon was the instrument, but the poem traces the cause to the LORD's judgment on sin.

options.text: Because God had forgotten His covenant with her.
options.note: The ruin fulfills the covenant warnings; God has not forgotten but has kept His word.

quiz.q: What refrain runs through the chapter like a tolling bell?

options.text: There is no one to comfort her; every human comforter has failed.
options.note: The word nacham, comfort, recurs, and its absence is the ache of the whole book.

options.text: That Zion weeps and finds no one to help her.
options.note: A fair paraphrase, though the specific, repeated cry is the lack of a comforter.

options.text: That the harvest had failed across the land.
options.note: Famine is present, but the repeated refrain is the absence of comfort.

options.text: That the enemies were about to repent.
options.note: The enemies gloat; there is no hint of their repentance.

quiz.q: How does Zion respond in the second half of the poem, 1:12 to 22?

options.text: She speaks for herself, confesses her rebellion, calls the LORD righteous, and pleads with Him to see her sorrow.
options.note: The voice shifts to Zion, who owns her guilt and turns her grief toward God.

options.text: She cries out to God about her suffering and her sin.
options.note: True, and more precisely she both confesses guilt and appeals for God to look and act.

options.text: She curses God and turns away from Him entirely.
options.note: She laments bitterly but keeps turning toward the LORD, not away from Him.

options.text: She declares that she has done nothing wrong.
options.note: She confesses she rebelled and that the LORD is righteous.

quiz.q: How does this chapter point forward to Christ?

options.text: Its cry, Is there any sorrow like mine, and its longing for a comforter are answered in Jesus, the man of sorrows who bears God's anger and comforts His people.
options.note: Christ enters the forsaken place and becomes the comfort Zion could not find.

options.text: Jesus is the suffering one who grieves and brings comfort.
options.note: True, and the specific links are the man of sorrows bearing wrath and giving the Comforter.

options.text: It teaches that Jerusalem would never be inhabited again.
options.note: The poem mourns the present ruin; its forward reach is to Christ, not to permanent desolation.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ at all.
options.note: The New Testament reads the man of sorrows and the Comforter as the answer to this grief.

questions: The poem begins with a single stunned word, How. When has grief left you without words? What does it mean that God gives His people inspired songs for exactly those moments?

Zion had many lovers, allies and idols she trusted, and every one of them betrayed her in the crisis. What are you leaning on for security instead of the LORD, and what happens to it when trouble comes?
The hardest honesty in this chapter is the confession the LORD is righteous, yet I rebelled. Where do you need to stop blaming circumstances or others and own your own sin before God?
Five times we hear there is no one to comfort her. Where are you aching for a comfort that no person or possession has been able to give, and how does Jesus meet that ache?
Even while grieving, Zion keeps crying Look, O LORD. How might turning your sorrow into honest prayer, rather than silence or despair, change the way you carry a hard season?

translationNotes.note: How translates eykah, the mourner's cry that opens the poem and gives the book its Hebrew name; it carries stunned grief more than a simple question.
The clause rendered they have seen her nakedness can also be rendered they have seen her shame; either way it pictures Jerusalem's disgrace laid bare before onlookers.
Most Hebrew manuscripts read my transgressions are bound into a yoke; some manuscripts and the Septuagint read He kept watch over my sins. The confession of guilt stands either way.
